sections.h2: Where is Kershaw County, SC, and how is it laid out?
sections.html:
Kershaw County is in north-central South Carolina, part of the Columbia metropolitan area, with Camden as its county seat and largest community. It covers 740.26 square miles, of which 726.61 are land, and it touches Lancaster, Chesterfield, Darlington, Sumter, Lee, Richland and Fairfield counties.

Interstate 20 crosses the county, along with U.S. 1, 521 and 601. Other named places include Lugoff, Elgin, Kershaw, Liberty Hill, Westville and Cassatt. About 52.8 percent of residents live in rural areas, so a Kershaw County house can mean a lot in Camden or several acres out toward Lake Wateree.

The 2020 census counted 65,403 people, up from 61,697 in 2010, and the 2025 estimate is 73,166.

sections.h2: What is the history behind Kershaw County?
sections.html:
Camden was settled around 1732 and is described as the oldest inland city in South Carolina. Kershaw County was created in 1791 and named for Col. Joseph Kershaw. From about 1800 to 1867 it was called Kershaw District.

The British held Camden from June 1780 to May 1781, and the Battle of Camden in August 1780 was a major American defeat. Union troops under Sherman burned parts of the town in February 1865. From the 1880s, northern families wintered in Camden, which built the horse culture that continues with the Carolina Cup steeplechase at Springdale Race Course. DuPont opened an Orlon plant in 1950 that was the largest employer for decades until production ended in 1990.

That history means older houses and old lots, and sometimes old deeds. Sellers who inherited a Camden home should expect the title search to go back through several owners.

sections.h2: What drives the Kershaw County economy?
sections.html:
Retail, health care and manufacturing lead local employment. In the third quarter of 2023 the county had 16,741 jobs at an average annual wage of $45,472. The largest sectors were retail trade at 3,653 jobs, health care and social assistance at 2,497, and manufacturing at 2,392.

sections.h2: Who handles property tax in Kershaw County?
sections.html:
Kershaw County splits property tax among three offices at the Kershaw County Government Center in Camden: the Assessor in Room 100, the Auditor in Room 120, and the Treasurer in Room 140. The Assessor values real property and mobile homes, measures new construction, takes value appeals and processes 4 percent legal residence and agricultural applications. The Auditor handles homestead exemptions. The Treasurer collects real and personal taxes and fees, and issues motor vehicle decals.

  • Treasurer phone: (803) 425-1529.
  • Delinquent tax questions go to the Delinquent Tax Collector at the same number, extension 4.
  • The Assessor's page does not list hours, so call first.
  • County reassessment follows the state's five-year cycle.

State law sets a penalty on unpaid taxes after the due date, with added percentages in February and March and an execution after that. You can read the penalty rules in Section 12-45-180. Ask the Treasurer for this year's exact dates before you plan a closing around them.

sections.h2: How do you appeal a Kershaw County assessment?
sections.html:
You object in writing to the Assessor within 90 days after the assessor mails the assessment notice. In a year with no notice, you may appeal in writing at any time; an appeal made before the first penalty date applies to that tax year.

  1. Request a conference. The Assessor must schedule it within 30 days of the request, or as soon as practical.
  2. File a written protest within 30 days after the conference.
  3. Expect a written response, generally within 30 days of the protest.
  4. Appeal to the county Board of Assessment Appeals within 30 days of that response.
  5. Ask for a contested case hearing in the Administrative Law Court within 30 days of the Board's written decision.

If the case is not resolved by December 31, the Assessor tells the auditor to adjust the bill to 80 percent of the protested amount, and any difference is settled with interest after the final decision. These steps come from Sections 12-60-2510 to 12-60-2550. The Kershaw County home page carried a notice headed "Appeal Deadline for Reassessment Notices" with no dates in the text we read, so check it for the current window.

sections.h2: What is the 4 percent legal residence rate in Kershaw County?
sections.html:
An owner-occupied home that is the owner's legal residence, with up to five contiguous acres, is taxed on 4 percent of its fair market value rather than 6 percent. You must apply on or before the first penalty date for the first year of the claim, and the home cannot be rented for more than 72 days in a calendar year.

A buyer of your house does not inherit your status; they must file their own. Section 12-43-220 also sets a penalty of 100 percent of the tax if someone holds the rate wrongly. Agricultural land can qualify at 4 percent in some cases, and a change of use brings rollback taxes for the current year and the three before it. The rules sit in Chapter 43 of Title 12.

State law also lets owners get a notice when value or classification changes by $1,000 or more.

sections.h2: What does a Kershaw County deed cost at closing?
sections.html:
South Carolina charges a deed fee of $1.85 for each $500 of value, split $1.30 to the state and $0.55 to the county, and the seller is generally liable for it.

Deeds back to a lender through foreclosure or a deed in lieu are exempt, as are quitclaim deeds that only confirm title with no payment. The details are in Title 12, Chapter 24. Call the office that records your deed for its current fee and any form requirements.

sections.h2: What should a Kershaw County seller know about land and houses?
sections.html:
Ask the county planning office and your insurer.

One local fact is worth knowing: between December 2021 and December 2022, southeastern Kershaw County recorded over 80 small earthquakes, six above magnitude 3.0 and the largest at 3.6. Ask your insurer and a local inspector what it means for a house you plan to sell.

  • Camden Military Academy and Woodward Field (the county airport) are local landmarks.
  • Historic events, including Revolutionary War Field Days in early November, draw visitors to Camden.
  • Acreage sales may involve agricultural classification and rollback taxes.
  • Inherited homes may need the estate opened before a clean deed can be signed.

Cash Home Buyers can look at a Kershaw County house as it stands, with back taxes, a delinquent account or a tenant in place, and walk through what a sale would involve.

faqs.q: Where do I pay property taxes in Kershaw County?
faqs.a: Pay the Treasurer in Room 140 of the Kershaw County Government Center in Camden, or use the payment link on the Treasurer's page. The office number is (803) 425-1529.

faqs.q: How long do I have to appeal my Kershaw County assessment?
faqs.a: You have 90 days after the Assessor mails the assessment notice to object in writing. After the Assessor's response you have 30 days to appeal to the Board of Assessment Appeals.

faqs.q: Who gives the homestead exemption in Kershaw County?
faqs.a: The Auditor, in Room 120, handles homestead exemptions. The Assessor handles the 4 percent legal residence rate and agricultural applications.

faqs.q: How often does Kershaw County reassess property?
faqs.a: The county is reassessed every five years, as the SC Department of Revenue requires. State law also requires notice when value or classification changes by $1,000 or more.

faqs.q: What happens to Kershaw County taxes if I sell my house?
faqs.a: Taxes owed for the year are normally paid out of the sale proceeds at closing. Ask the Treasurer for a payoff figure, and the buyer should file their own legal residence application.
